1: # Testing
2: 
3: celld makes three important promises:
4: 
5: - An acknowledged write is durable.
6: - A cell has one writer at a time. It never has two.
7: - Code written for Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects operates the
8:   same on celld.
9: 
10: We try to break each promise at the layer where a failure shows most
11: clearly. We test the API contract with differential execution against the
12: Cloudflare runtime. We check the coordination protocol against an
13: exhaustively model-checked specification, and we test it with
14: deterministic simulation. We test the full system with fault injection
15: on live fleets.
16: 
17: ## Conformance: two runtimes, one output
18: 
19: We test the compatibility promise differentially. We run each Workers and
20: Durable Objects program twice: once on workerd, the runtime binary that
21: Cloudflare operates in production, and once on celld, on identical bytes.
22: The two outputs must be equal. This shows two facts at once: the program
23: is real Cloudflare code, because workerd accepts it, and celld obeys the
24: contract, because the outputs are equal. A test cannot agree with our own
25: runtime by accident.
26: 
27: The corpus only grows. When celld gets a new API surface, we add fixtures
28: for that surface, and the fixtures must give equal output on the two
29: engines. We also port test suites from workerd itself: the Durable
30: Objects contract, the web-platform globals, and the upstream Web Platform
31: Tests. Before a release, we also replay scenarios through the full
32: `celld` binary in each deployment mode: storage, SQL, alarms, streams,
33: WebSockets, and lifecycle.
34: 
35: ## Specification: exhaustive at small size
36: 
37: The coordination protocol is also specified in TLA+. Heyang Zhou wrote
38: the specifications against celld v0.1.0, and his model checking found
39: four bugs and a split-brain that lost an acknowledged write. All are
40: fixed. None had surfaced in our own review or testing.
41: 
42: Where simulation samples schedules, the checker enumerates them: at a
43: small configuration it visits every reachable state. The model grants
44: the implementation a linearizable object store and perfect shared
45: clocks, so a violation it finds needs no clock skew and no storage
46: anomaly to occur. The invariants are the first two promises at the top
47: of this page: one writer for each epoch, and no acknowledged write
48: lost. The fencing argument itself — that a stale owner's late writes
49: cannot cost an acknowledged write, because the epoch in the key keeps
50: its lineage apart — is checked, not asserted.
51: 
52: Every configuration carries a pinned expected verdict, and most of the
53: verdicts are failures: each failing configuration models a bug the
54: protocol once had, or a deliberately broken checker, and the model
55: must produce the counterexample. A configuration that stops failing
56: has lost its tooth. One tooth had already fallen out when the
57: specifications arrived; we repaired it.
58: 
59: Some specifications model a proposed protocol before it is built. When
60: the fence on write acknowledgments was redesigned, the design-stage
61: check produced an eight-state counterexample against the version it
62: replaced: a dormant cell resumes at its old epoch while its release is
63: in flight, acknowledges a write, and the takeover that follows
64: restores without it. The fix shipped; the counterexample stays as a
65: pinned failure.
66: 
67: The checker has also removed code: celld once sealed a cell's durable
68: history at restore, and the verdicts showed the seal defended only the
69: return of a write that was never acknowledged — an outcome celld does
70: not promise to prevent — while its permanent cut could turn a
71: recoverable ordering slip into a permanent loss. The seal is gone.
72: 
73: The specifications are a hand-synced snapshot, deliberately not in
74: continuous integration: a silently stale gate is worse than none. In
75: practice their updates have landed in the same changes that moved the
76: protocol, and a delta ledger records what the model does not yet
77: describe, including places where the model is weaker than the code
78: rather than wrong. Simulation remains the per-commit ratchet; the
79: model is its exhaustive small-configuration complement.
80: 
81: ## Simulation: the protocol under adversarial schedules
82: 
83: The dangerous bugs live in the coordination: a crash during an ownership
84: handoff, a lease renewal that races a takeover, an alarm that fires
85: against a partially restored cell. These windows are nanoseconds wide and
86: open rarely, so a test cannot wait for them.
87: 
88: Thus the coordination protocol is a
89: [pure decision core](https://github.com/denoland/celld/tree/main/crates/logic)
90: with no I/O of its own: the clock, the randomness, and the object store
91: are interfaces, and a simulator drives the core. The simulated store
92: injects latency, compare-and-swap races, and lost responses; the clocks
93: drift apart; a node can crash at each await point. Scripted adversaries
94: play the cells: a handler that never returns, a write stream that stops
95: halfway. V8 stays out of the simulation, because V8 is not deterministic.
96: 
97: A seeded scheduler drives each run, so a failure is not a fluke: the seed
98: replays it exactly, every time, and we keep the seed until the bug is
99: dead. We examine each property for safety (two writers in one epoch, a
100: lost acknowledged write, an expired lease that comes back) and for
101: liveness (each armed alarm fires, and ownership settles on one node after
102: a crash). A property must survive tens of thousands of seeds, and the
103: core protocols have run through millions of different schedules.
104: 
105: Simulation has a known failure mode: the checker that cannot fail. So
106: we also test the checkers: we run deliberately broken variants of the
107: protocol against the properties, and the properties must find the damage.
108: A suite that stays green against a broken protocol is a broken suite.
109: 
110: ## Live fleets: what simulation cannot see
111: 
112: Simulation cannot see the real S3 tail latency, the real kernel and
113: filesystem behavior, or V8 under memory pressure. The third layer is
114: therefore a permanent fleet lab: standard VMs from standard providers,
115: and a real bucket. The workloads rotate: chat rooms under many WebSocket
116: connections, working sets that shift across tens of thousands of cells
117: (each cell has a unique checksum), deployment cutovers under load, and
118: runs that fill the nodes to the memory limit. The lab qualifies each
119: release, and between releases it pushes the density and the fault
120: coverage further. Each run makes an archived evidence bundle: the
121: configuration, the verification sweeps, the node journals, the kernel
122: logs, and the phase timings. We keep a red run with the same care as a
123: green run, because a failure that the harness caught is a result, not a
124: retry.
125: 
126: We inject the faults between verification passes. A pass fetches each
127: cell through different nodes and compares the durable state exactly: the
128: status, the body, and the full message ledger. Each run therefore has a
129: clean picture before the fault and after it. A cell can be unavailable
130: for a short time while its ownership moves, but its committed state must
131: stay complete, and a live node must serve that state again.
132: 
133: The scenarios attack every seam that we know:
134: 
135: - Stop a node with `SIGKILL` in the middle of a write stream and delete
136:   its local database, so recovery can only come from the bucket. Every
137:   acknowledged write comes back, because the output gate held each
138:   response until the write was durable.
139: - Freeze an owner node, write to its cells through other nodes, and
140:   unfreeze it. The node sees that its lease moved and refuses to serve
141:   the old state, and each write from the other nodes lands exactly one
142:   time: one epoch has at most one writer.
143: - Cut a node off from the bucket. It fences itself, because a node that
144:   cannot replicate must not own cells.
145: - Throttle the bucket, so it answers each request with a 429. The engine
146:   slows to the write rate of the store and does not amplify the
147:   throttle, because a node that knows its replicated position does not
148:   ask a slow store for extra listings.
149: - Stop a full host at the provider level in the middle of a workload.
150:   Its cells move to the other nodes, and the returning host joins again
151:   with no duplicate residency.
152: 
153: Across every run of every scenario, no acknowledged write was lost and
154: no committed state was damaged; the verification sweeps show zero body
155: faults, zero status faults, and zero lost messages.
156: 
157: ## A few numbers we trust
158: 
159: Each number includes the condition of its measurement. A number without
160: its conditions has no value.
161: 
162: - **The epoch fence holds under contention.** Five hundred claimants
163:   tried at the same time to own the same cells: 5,500 attempts, one
164:   writer for each epoch, zero violations.
165: - **A warm resident request is local.** A request to a resident cell does
166:   zero bucket operations and returns in p50 ~1.1 ms and p99 ~7 ms (a
167:   fixed-host measurement). Only a cold activation touches object storage.
168: - **A durable write waits for a durability proof.** A single node proves
169:   each write through the bucket, so one storage round trip is the minimum
170:   latency for that write. A fleet of two or more nodes can prove a write
171:   when each follower holds it on disk, and a follower fsync is much
172:   faster than a storage round trip: a lab fleet measured about 600 ms for
173:   a bucket proof and about 25 ms for a fleet proof. The bucket upload
174:   races every fleet proof and either one proves the write, so a slow
175:   follower cannot make a write slower than a bucket proof. Concurrent
176:   writes to one cell join one shared upload, so the throughput of one
177:   cell is not one round trip for each write.
178: - **A restore is normal work.** Placement handles the restore of an
179:   inactive cell as ordinary work, and not as an emergency procedure. The
180:   measured restore times come from the retired external replicator, so this
181:   page gives no number until a fleet run measures `celld-ltx`.
182: - **Ten small nodes held real scale.** A fleet of ten nodes, each with 4
183:   vCPU and 8 GB, held 10,000 resident cells and 20,000 concurrent
184:   WebSocket connections. We stopped two of the ten nodes, and the data of
185:   every cell was available again on another node in ~11 s at the tail
186:   (with reserve headroom).
187: 
188: ## The failure edges we intend to find
189: 
190: We must also know where a policy stops, so we record the edges instead of
191: tuning them away. The clearest edge is the reserve headroom: a fleet that
192: is full to its resident limit has no space for the cells of a lost node,
193: so a failure of more than one node at the limit degrades the service,
194: and a fleet with headroom does not. We measure both sides of that line,
195: the good restoration with reserve and the red case without, because this
196: measurement is part of the work.
197: 
198: If you find an edge that we did not find, tell us: a schedule that breaks
199: a promise, a fault that we did not inject, a number that you cannot
200: reproduce. That is exactly the bug report that we want:
201: [github.com/denoland/celld/issues](https://github.com/denoland/celld/issues).

(End of file - total 201 lines)
</content>

a crash). A property must survive tens of thousands of seeds, and the
core protocols have run through millions of different schedules.

Simulation has a known failure mode: the checker that cannot fail. So
we also test the checkers: we run deliberately broken variants of the
protocol against the properties, and the properties must find the damage.
A suite that stays green against a broken protocol is a broken suite.

## Live fleets: what simulation cannot see

Simulation cannot see the real S3 tail latency, the real kernel and
filesystem behavior, or V8 under memory pressure. The third layer is
therefore a permanent fleet lab: standard VMs from standard providers,
and a real bucket. The workloads rotate: chat rooms under many WebSocket
connections, working sets that shift across tens of thousands of cells
(each cell has a unique checksum), deployment cutovers under load, and
runs that fill the nodes to the memory limit. The lab qualifies each
release, and between releases it pushes the density and the fault
coverage further. Each run makes an archived evidence bundle: the
configuration, the verification sweeps, the node journals, the kernel
logs, and the phase timings. We keep a red run with the same care as a
green run, because a failure that the harness caught is a result, not a
retry.

We inject the faults between verification passes. A pass fetches each
cell through different nodes and compares the durable state exactly: the
status, the body, and the full message ledger. Each run therefore has a
clean picture before the fault and after it. A cell can be unavailable
for a short time while its ownership moves, but its committed state must
stay complete, and a live node must serve that state again.

The scenarios attack every seam that we know:

- Stop a node with `SIGKILL` in the middle of a write stream and delete
  its local database, so recovery can only come from the bucket. Every
  acknowledged write comes back, because the output gate held each
  response until the write was durable.
- Freeze an owner node, write to its cells through other nodes, and
  unfreeze it. The node sees that its lease moved and refuses to serve
  the old state, and each write from the other nodes lands exactly one
  time: one epoch has at most one writer.
- Cut a node off from the bucket. It fences itself, because a node that
  cannot replicate must not own cells.
- Throttle the bucket, so it answers each request with a 429. The engine
  slows to the write rate of the store and does not amplify the
  throttle, because a node that knows its replicated position does not
  ask a slow store for extra listings.
- Stop a full host at the provider level in the middle of a workload.
  Its cells move to the other nodes, and the returning host joins again
  with no duplicate residency.

Across every run of every scenario, no acknowledged write was lost and
no committed state was damaged; the verification sweeps show zero body
faults, zero status faults, and zero lost messages.

## A few numbers we trust

Each number includes the condition of its measurement. A number without
its conditions has no value.

- **The epoch fence holds under contention.** Five hundred claimants
  tried at the same time to own the same cells: 5,500 attempts, one
  writer for each epoch, zero violations.
- **A warm resident request is local.** A request to a resident cell does
  zero bucket operations and returns in p50 ~1.1 ms and p99 ~7 ms (a
  fixed-host measurement). Only a cold activation touches object storage.
- **A durable write waits for a durability proof.** A single node proves
  each write through the bucket, so one storage round trip is the minimum
  latency for that write. A fleet of two or more nodes can prove a write
  when each follower holds it on disk, and a follower fsync is much
  faster than a storage round trip: a lab fleet measured about 600 ms for
  a bucket proof and about 25 ms for a fleet proof. The bucket upload
  races every fleet proof and either one proves the write, so a slow
  follower cannot make a write slower than a bucket proof. Concurrent
  writes to one cell join one shared upload, so the throughput of one
  cell is not one round trip for each write.
- **A restore is normal work.** Placement handles the restore of an
  inactive cell as ordinary work, and not as an emergency procedure. The
  measured restore times come from the retired external replicator, so this
  page gives no number until a fleet run measures `celld-ltx`.
- **Ten small nodes held real scale.** A fleet of ten nodes, each with 4
  vCPU and 8 GB, held 10,000 resident cells and 20,000 concurrent
  WebSocket connections. We stopped two of the ten nodes, and the data of
  every cell was available again on another node in ~11 s at the tail
  (with reserve headroom).

## The failure edges we intend to find

We must also know where a policy stops, so we record the edges instead of
tuning them away. The clearest edge is the reserve headroom: a fleet that
is full to its resident limit has no space for the cells of a lost node,
so a failure of more than one node at the limit degrades the service,
and a fleet with headroom does not. We measure both sides of that line,
the good restoration with reserve and the red case without, because this
measurement is part of the work.

If you find an edge that we did not find, tell us: a schedule that breaks
a promise, a fault that we did not inject, a number that you cannot
reproduce. That is exactly the bug report that we want:
[github.com/denoland/celld/issues](https://github.com/denoland/celld/issues).

# Security

celld is an alpha. It is not safe for hostile multi-tenant use. Security fixes
apply to the latest release only, so older alpha builds do not receive fixes.

## Security boundary

One fleet runs one application, and celld trusts the application code, the fleet
nodes, and the operators. Application code can use its configured bindings and
can consume shared node resources. Do not run code from mutually distrusting
tenants in one fleet.

celld depends on two external security boundaries:

- A trusted private network protects the internal listener. Use an encrypted
  overlay when the private network does not provide confidentiality.
- Object storage credentials control the fleet. Give each credential access to
  one fleet bucket only.

## Separate the listeners

celld opens two HTTP listeners. The public listener serves the deployed Worker,
and the internal listener serves the peer protocol and the operator API.

Use `--listen` for the public listener. Expose this listener through a load
balancer, a reverse proxy, or a public firewall rule.

Use `--internal-listen` for the internal listener. Its default address is
`127.0.0.1:0`, so celld selects an available loopback port at each start. Use
`--advertise` to give peers an address that reaches this listener.

An explicit advertised address requires an explicit internal-listener address.
celld also rejects an explicit non-loopback public listener without an explicit
internal listener. These checks prevent an obsolete one-listener configuration.

celld cannot verify a hostname or a translated port. You must route the
advertised address to the internal listener, and you must not route it to the
public listener.

The public listener reserves only `/.well-known/celld/health`. A healthy node
returns a 200 response with `{"ok":true}`, and an unhealthy node returns a 503
response. The deployed Worker owns `/health` and every other public path.

The internal listener does not pass an unknown path to the Worker. It returns a
404 response, so an operator request cannot become an application request.

## Protect each surface

| Surface | Required protection |
| --- | --- |
| The public listener | Terminate TLS and authenticate users in a proxy or the application. |
| The internal listener | Restrict access to trusted operators and fleet nodes. Use an encrypted overlay when the private network does not provide confidentiality. |
| The fleet bucket | Restrict the credentials to one fleet bucket. |

The internal listener has three request groups:

- Most operator routes let an operator inspect or control a node without
  request authentication.
- The `/peer/tunnel` route establishes a tunnel for cell fetch, RPC, and
  WebSocket calls. The establishment request carries the fleet HMAC, a clock
  limit, and replay protection, so only a holder of the fleet secret can open
  a tunnel. Each call then crosses inside the tunnel as plain HTTP with the
  cell scope in a reserved header, and these inner calls are not signed.
- The peer-control routes coordinate fleet nodes, and the reserved-cell routes
  access runtime state. These routes use the fleet HMAC for request
  authentication, a clock limit, and replay protection.

All three groups require the trusted private network.

The tunnel permits a request body to stream to the owner, so the fleet HMAC
cannot sign an individual call. The establishment signature decides who can
open a tunnel, and a tunneled call can address an application class or a
runtime class, so every path to a runtime class demands the fleet secret.
The signature does not authenticate the bytes after the establishment, and
it does not encrypt any traffic. The private network must therefore stay
trusted, and the fleet HMAC does not replace this network boundary.

celld does not terminate TLS on either listener. Do not expose the internal
listener to the public internet. Use an encrypted overlay such as WireGuard or
Tailscale when the network does not provide the required confidentiality.

## Use the internal operator API

The internal operator API is available in the released binary. It is an alpha
interface, so a release can change its paths or response formats.

These routes do not authenticate the caller:

- `/state` reports node state.
- `/cell/<SCOPE>` resolves or activates a cell.
- `/evict/<SCOPE>` evicts a resident cell.
- `/do/<ID>` sends a direct request to an ordinary Durable Object.
- `POST /shutdown` starts a graceful ownership handoff. The
  `handoff=preserve` query prepares a same-node reload.

The `/do/<ID>` route refuses every reserved runtime class. These classes include
D1, Workflows, KV, and Queues. Their operator protocols can access application
data or change runtime state, so they use the HMAC-authenticated
`/runtime/<SCOPE>` route.

`/peer/probe` returns a signed diagnostic response. The peer protocol also
uses other reserved internal paths. An operator must not call these paths
directly.

## Set the forwarded-header policy

celld ignores `X-Forwarded-Host` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` by default. Set
`--trust-forwarded-headers` or `CELLD_TRUST_FORWARDED_HEADERS=1` only when a
trusted proxy replaces both headers. celld uses the last value in each header,
so an earlier client value does not override the proxy value.

celld always takes the path and query from the request target. It ignores the
scheme and authority in an absolute-form target, so a client cannot bypass the
host policy through the request line.

Without a trusted proxy, the `Host` header controls the hostname in
`request.url`. celld accepts a hostname, an IPv4 address, or a bracketed IPv6
address, with an optional port. It rejects malformed and noncanonical values,
and it uses `celld.local` when no source gives a valid host.

These checks keep the path and query valid, but they do not make the hostname
trustworthy. An application must not use an unchecked hostname for an
authorization decision. Use a trusted proxy or check the hostname against a
list in the Worker.

## Limit request bodies

The public Worker listener and `/do/<ID>` have a 1 GiB request body limit by
default. Set `CELLD_MAX_REQUEST_BODY_BYTES` to a smaller positive value to
change the limit. celld returns status 413 for a declared oversized body and
when a Worker reads past the limit.

For a method other than `GET` or `HEAD`, `/do/<ID>` streams a body when its
declared length is at least 1 MiB or its length is unknown. celld collects each
smaller body before dispatch.

## Protect the fleet bucket

The fleet bucket is the root of authority for the fleet. It stores the
deployments, the cell state, the ownership leases, the node leases, and the
shared peer-authentication secret.

A person who holds the bucket credentials controls the fleet. Give each
credential access to one fleet bucket only, and replace a credential after a
suspected disclosure.

## Understand cell ownership

Each cell is a SQLite database with one writer. One node owns a cell at a time,
and an ownership epoch fences each cell. A node that loses its lease cannot
modify the current cell state.

This fencing protects storage consistency, but it does not isolate hostile
applications. See [what celld guarantees](guarantees.md) for the storage protocol,
and see [limitations](limitations.md) for the complete alpha boundary.

1: # Telemetry
2: 
3: celld can record traces and logs for the requests it serves. The
4: feature is off by default, and the off state costs nothing. Set
5: `CELLD_OTEL=1` to turn it on.
6: 
7: The default sink is the fleet bucket. celld writes Parquet files under
8: the `telemetry/` prefix, so a fleet with a bucket has observability
9: with no other service. DuckDB can query these files directly. An
10: alternative sink sends the same data to an OpenTelemetry collector.
11: 
12: The schema is version `v0-unstable`. The column names can change
13: before a stable release, and each file carries the schema version in
14: its object metadata.
15: 
16: ## Configuration
17: 
18: | variable | default | effect |
19: | --- | --- | --- |
20: | `CELLD_OTEL` | `0` | Set this value to `1` to enable telemetry. |
21: | `CELLD_OTEL_SINK` | `bucket` | `bucket` writes Parquet to the fleet bucket. `otlp` sends OTLP/HTTP protobuf to a collector instead. |
22: | `CELLD_OTEL_BUCKET` | the fleet bucket | A different bucket for the Parquet files, on the same endpoint and credentials. |
23: | `CELLD_OTEL_RETENTION` | `30d` | celld deletes telemetry files older than this. `none` disables the deletion, so your own lifecycle rules can control the data. |
24: | `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_MS` | `300000` | celld writes a Parquet file after this many milliseconds of buffered events. |
25: | `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_BYTES` | `5242880` | celld writes a Parquet file after the buffered events reach this many bytes. celld uses the limit it reaches first. |
26: | `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER` | `parentbased_always_on` | A standard sampler name. `traceidratio` with `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG` records a fraction of the traces. |
27: | `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | `http://localhost:4318` | The collector base URL, for the `otlp` sink. `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` and `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT` also apply. |
28: | `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` | `celld` | The service name in the exported resource. |
29: 
30: The `bucket` sink requires the node to have a fleet bucket
31: (`CELLD_BUCKET`). The `otlp` sink works on a node without one.
32: 
33: ## What celld records
34: 
35: celld records a span for each request a stateless Worker serves, for
36: each event a cell serves (a fetch, an alarm, an RPC, a WebSocket
37: message), for each outbound `fetch()`, and for each cell start. A
38: span carries the request id, the cell, the isolate, the
39: queue wait, the outbound URL and status, and the durability facts the
40: runtime already knows.
41: 
42: celld also records each `console.log` line as a log record. The log
43: record carries the trace id and the span id of the handler that wrote
44: it, so a query can join the logs to the traces. The correlation

display.text:
# Telemetry

celld can record traces and logs for the requests it serves. The
feature is off by default, and the off state costs nothing. Set
`CELLD_OTEL=1` to turn it on.

The default sink is the fleet bucket. celld writes Parquet files under
the `telemetry/` prefix, so a fleet with a bucket has observability
with no other service. DuckDB can query these files directly. An
alternative sink sends the same data to an OpenTelemetry collector.

The schema is version `v0-unstable`. The column names can change
before a stable release, and each file carries the schema version in
its object metadata.

## Configuration

| variable | default | effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CELLD_OTEL` | `0` | Set this value to `1` to enable telemetry. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_SINK` | `bucket` | `bucket` writes Parquet to the fleet bucket. `otlp` sends OTLP/HTTP protobuf to a collector instead. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_BUCKET` | the fleet bucket | A different bucket for the Parquet files, on the same endpoint and credentials. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_RETENTION` | `30d` | celld deletes telemetry files older than this. `none` disables the deletion, so your own lifecycle rules can control the data. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_MS` | `300000` | celld writes a Parquet file after this many milliseconds of buffered events. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_BYTES` | `5242880` | celld writes a Parquet file after the buffered events reach this many bytes. celld uses the limit it reaches first. |
| `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER` | `parentbased_always_on` | A standard sampler name. `traceidratio` with `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG` records a fraction of the traces. |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | `http://localhost:4318` | The collector base URL, for the `otlp` sink. `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` and `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT` also apply. |
| `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` | `celld` | The service name in the exported resource. |

The `bucket` sink requires the node to have a fleet bucket
(`CELLD_BUCKET`). The `otlp` sink works on a node without one.

## What celld records

celld records a span for each request a stateless Worker serves, for
each event a cell serves (a fetch, an alarm, an RPC, a WebSocket
message), for each outbound `fetch()`, and for each cell start. A
span carries the request id, the cell, the isolate, the
queue wait, the outbound URL and status, and the durability facts the
runtime already knows.

celld also records each `console.log` line as a log record. The log
record carries the trace id and the span id of the handler that wrote
it, so a query can join the logs to the traces. The correlation
survives `await`.

celld reads the W3C `traceparent` header on incoming requests, so its
spans join the trace of the system in front of it. celld sends a
`traceparent` header on outbound `fetch()`, so downstream systems can
join too. A Worker call to a Durable Object stays in one trace.

The sampler decides at the start of a request. An unsampled request
records nothing and costs almost nothing. Under load, telemetry sheds
before requests do, and celld counts what it sheds.

celld records no metrics yet. The spans carry the durations and the
queue waits, so many questions a metric answers have an answer in the
traces, and a metrics signal can come later without a change to the
trace schema.

## Query the bucket with DuckDB

```sql
INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;
CREATE SECRET celld_telemetry (
  TYPE s3, KEY_ID '...', SECRET '...',
  ENDPOINT 's3.example.com', URL_STYLE 'path'
);
CREATE VIEW traces AS SELECT * FROM
  read_parquet('s3://YOUR-BUCKET/telemetry/traces/*/*/*/*/*/*.parquet');
CREATE VIEW logs AS SELECT * FROM
  read_parquet('s3://YOUR-BUCKET/telemetry/logs/*/*/*/*/*/*.parquet');

-- The slowest requests.
SELECT name, duration_us, trace_id FROM traces
  ORDER BY duration_us DESC LIMIT 20;

-- Every log line, inside the span that wrote it.
SELECT l.body, t.name, t.duration_us FROM logs l
  JOIN traces t ON l.trace_id = t.trace_id AND l.span_id = t.span_id;
```

An S3-compatible endpoint such as minio needs `URL_STYLE 'path'` in
the secret, and a plain-HTTP endpoint also needs `USE_SSL false`. AWS
itself does not need either.

The files are partitioned by node and by hour:
`telemetry/traces/<node>/<yyyy>/<mm>/<dd>/<hh>/<id>.parquet`. A query
that reads one day therefore touches only that day's files.

## File size and compaction

celld writes one Parquet file for each flush, on a time limit or a
size limit, whichever it reaches first. The defaults are 5 minutes
(`CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_MS=300000`) and 5 MB (`CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_BYTES=5242880`).

Keep the defaults if you run no compaction job. They make files large
enough for a fast query with no other moving part. A query sees an
event up to 5 minutes after the request, so the default suits an
investigation after the fact.

Set `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_MS=10000` for a near-live view, such as a
dashboard or an active debug session: a query then sees an event
within 10 seconds. A short flush makes many small files, and DuckDB
opens every file a query reads, so you must also run the compaction
job below. Turn on the compaction job first, then shorten the flush,
or queries grow slow within hours.

The `otlp` sink is the other route to a near-live view. It sends each
batch to a collector, so set the same short `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_MS`.

## Compaction

Run a compaction job on a maintenance node, not on a celld node. celld
does not compact its own files, because the serving path must not do
storage maintenance and each node writes only the files it produced.

The job rewrites one past hour of small files into one large file.
DuckDB does the work:

```sql
COPY (
  SELECT * FROM
    read_parquet('s3://YOUR-BUCKET/telemetry/traces/<node>/2026/08/09/22/*.parquet')
  ORDER BY start_unix_us
) TO 's3://YOUR-BUCKET/telemetry/traces/<node>/2026/08/09/22/compacted.parquet'
  (FORMAT parquet, COMPRESSION zstd);
```

Run the job once an hour, for the hour that just ended. Do not compact
the current hour, because a node still writes to it. Delete the source
files after DuckDB writes the compacted file. The compacted file is
also smaller, because zstd compresses one sorted batch better than
many separate files.

display.text:
# WebAssembly

A Worker bundle can import a `.wasm` file. The import gives the
compiled module, not the bytes. This is the same rule that Wrangler
applies, so a bundle that runs on Cloudflare runs on celld without a
change.

```js
import addModule from "./add.wasm";

const { exports } = new WebAssembly.Instance(addModule);

export default {
  fetch() {
    return new Response(String(exports.add(2, 3)));
  },
};
```

`celld deploy` finds each wasm import, uploads the file beside the
bundle, and marks the deployment with the `wasm-v1` feature. A node
that predates this feature refuses the deployment with a clear
message, so a mixed fleet fails at deploy time and not at request
time.

celld compiles each wasm module once for the whole process. Every
isolate after the first one reuses the compiled module, so a cell
activation does not pay the compilation again.

## Rust with workers-rs

[workers-rs](https://github.com/cloudflare/workers-rs) compiles a Rust
crate to a Worker. The tool `worker-build` produces a JavaScript shim
and a wasm file, and the shim is a normal entry point for
`celld deploy`.

1. Install the build tool: `cargo install worker-build`.
2. Build the crate: `worker-build --release`.
3. Point the config at the shim:

```jsonc
{
  "name": "my-app",
  "main": "./build/worker/shim.mjs",
  "compatibility_date": "2026-01-01",
}
```

4. Deploy: `celld deploy`.

The shim wraps its exports in a JavaScript Proxy, and celld resolves
entrypoint classes and Durable Object classes through that wrapper.
The runtime surface that the application can use is the surface in
[Cloudflare compatibility](cloudflare-compat.md); a workers-rs API
that maps to a missing runtime feature does not work.

## The Worker Loader

A dynamically loaded worker can also carry wasm. Pass the bytes in the
`modules` map; a `BufferSource` value becomes a compiled-module import
in the loaded worker.

```js
const worker = env.loader.load({
  mainModule: "main.js",
  modules: {
    "main.js": `import m from "./add.wasm"; ...`,
    "add.wasm": wasmBytes,
  },
});
```

## Limits

The wasm bytes count against the deployment size limits, exactly as
JavaScript modules do. A wasm module that does not compile fails the
importing module with a `WebAssembly.CompileError` that names the
file.

323: /// on `Channel` inside `celld-logic` would split one output invariant into a
324: /// separate rule for each channel.
325: ///
326: /// An alarm is missing here on purpose, and stays missing. Its consuming
327: /// commit does open a barrier -- as `GateOwner::Alarm`, keyed by the cell and
328: /// epoch the firing was dispatched against -- but a barrier is not a channel.
329: /// The alarm's settlement is not an egress: it is replayed back into the core
330: /// rather than released to the shell, it has no request to route by, and the
331: /// output gate does not release it to the shell, and it has no request to route
332: /// by. A variant here would force the core to match on `Channel` to tell a
333: /// release from a replay, which is the one thing this enum exists to prevent.
334: #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash)]
335: pub enum Channel {
336:     /// The answer to the cell event itself: an HTTP response, a cell RPC
337:     /// reply, or a peer-served reply.
338:     Response,
339:     /// `fetch()` from a handler to a third party.
340:     Fetch,
341:     /// A frame from a `webSocketMessage` handler, captured by the host and
342:     /// released from the cell's barrier queue.
343:     WsHibernatable,
344:     /// A frame on a socket the isolate opened and polls itself. It cannot be
345:     /// captured, because the handler may be awaiting the reply to the very
346:     /// frame being held, so it waits on a durability ticket instead.
347:     WsSelf,
348:     /// A service-binding call, `env.NAME.fetch()` or its RPC form.
349:     Service,
350:     /// A call to another cell: its `fetch` or one of its RPC methods.
351:     CellRpc,
352:     /// A leased Queue batch leaving its broker for a consumer Worker.
353:     Queue,
354: }
355: 
356: impl Channel {
357:     /// Return the diagnostic name for this channel.
358:     pub fn as_str(self) -> &'static str {
359:         match self {
360:             Channel::Response => "response",
361:             Channel::Fetch => "fetch",
362:             Channel::WsHibernatable => "ws_hibernatable",
363:             Channel::WsSelf => "ws_self",
364:             Channel::Service => "service",
365:             Channel::CellRpc => "cellrpc",
366:             Channel::Queue => "queue",
367:         }
368:     }
369: }

480:         now_mono_ms: u64,
481:     },

483:     /// shell falls back to the stateless pool when no resident is available;
484:     /// choosing and pinning a resident is lifecycle policy and therefore
485:     /// belongs in the replayable core.

487:         request: RequestId,
488:     },

490:     /// leaving published runtimes and ownership intact. Late shell completions
491:     /// are stale, so a long restore cannot consume the complete shutdown grace

501:     /// this cell's state. The core withholds it until every write it can
502:     /// reveal is proven durable. This is the output gate, and the whole of it:
503:     /// every channel arrives here and the core does not branch on which.
504:     ///

540:         op: OpId,
541:         result: Result<(), Failure>,

547:     },

558:     },

562:         /// core opens for the consuming commit is keyed by these, and not by

566:         cell: CellId,
567:         epoch: Epoch,
568:         now_ms: u64,
569:         now_mono_ms: u64,
570:         /// The deadline standing after the handler ran, whether a wake entry

572:         /// wrote. The position is sampled last, so it covers the consume

577:         cell: CellId,
578:     },
579:     WakeHintAt {
580:         cell: CellId,
581:         now_mono_ms: u64,
582:     },

589:         result: Result<Option<OwnerRecord>, Failure>,
590:     },
591:     NodeLogRecovered {
592:         op: OpId,
593:         result: Result<(), Failure>,
594:     },

600:         now_mono_ms: u64,
601:     },

603:         op: OpId,
604:         now_ms: u64,
605:         result: Result<Option<NodeLeaseRecord>, Failure>,
606:     },

608:         op: OpId,
609:         now_ms: u64,
610:         result: Result<Vec<CapacityPeer>, Failure>,
611:     },
612:     OwnerCasCompleted {
613:         op: OpId,
614:         result: Result<CasOutcome, Failure>,
615:     },

617:         op: OpId,
618:         result: Result<CasOutcome, Failure>,
619:     },

623:         op: OpId,
624:         result: Result<AdoptedCell, Failure>,

929: #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
930: pub enum StopCause {
931:     Cleanup,
932:     /// `rebalance` means this eviction hands the cell to the fleet: its
933:     /// ownership record is released and the local replica is not worth
934:     /// keeping. An idle eviction is the opposite on both counts -- it
935:     /// keeps the record so the next activation here renames the file into
936:     /// place instead of paying a full remote restore.
937:     Evict {
938:         rebalance: bool,
939:     },
940:     Fence,
941:     /// A durability proof came back negative, so this runtime's memory and its
942:     /// local database may hold writes the bucket does not. celld has just told

# LTX file format (Version 3) — byte layout

Derived from `superfly/ltx` v0.5.2 (`ltx.go`, `checksum.go`, `encoder.go`, and
`decoder.go`). The implementation is in `src/ltx.rs`. All multi-byte integers
are **big-endian**.

## File structure

```
+----------------------+
| Header   (100 bytes) |
+----------------------+
| Page 0               |   PageHeader(6) + Size(4) + LZ4-block(page data)
| Page 1               |
| ...                  |
+----------------------+
| Empty PageHeader (6) |   pgno=0 — terminates the page block
+----------------------+
| Page index           |   varint tuples + end marker + u64 size
+----------------------+
| Trailer  (16 bytes)  |
+----------------------+
```

## Header (100 bytes)

| Offset | Size | Field | Notes |
|-------:|-----:|-------|-------|
| 0  | 4 | Magic | ASCII `"LTX1"` |
| 4  | 4 | Flags (u32) | only `HeaderFlagNoChecksum = 1<<1` is valid |
| 8  | 4 | PageSize (u32) | power of two, 512..=65536 |
| 12 | 4 | Commit (u32) | DB size after txn, in pages |
| 16 | 8 | MinTXID (u64) | |
| 24 | 8 | MaxTXID (u64) | |
| 32 | 8 | Timestamp (i64) | ms since unix epoch |
| 40 | 8 | PreApplyChecksum (u64) | 0 on snapshots (MinTXID==1) |
| 48 | 8 | WALOffset (i64) | 0 if journal |
| 56 | 8 | WALSize (i64) | 0 if journal |
| 64 | 4 | WALSalt1 (u32) | |
| 68 | 4 | WALSalt2 (u32) | |
| 72 | 8 | NodeID (u64) | |
| 80 | 20 | (reserved) | zero |

`IsSnapshot() == (MinTXID == 1)`. Snapshots include all pages and have
`PreApplyChecksum == 0`.

## Page block

Each v0.5.2 page contains a `PageHeader`, a four-byte compressed size, and one
independent raw LZ4 block. The writer uses the fast compressor from
`pierrec/lz4` v4.1.23. The block ends with an **empty PageHeader**
(`pgno == 0`).

**PageHeader (6 bytes):** `Pgno (u32 @0)`, `Flags (u16 @4)`. The
`PageHeaderFlagSize` bit (`1<<0`) marks the size-prefixed block representation.
No other flag is valid.

Files written through LTX v0.5.1 have a zero page flag and one independent LZ4
frame after each page header. A v0.5.2 decoder accepts both representations,
so existing Litestream objects remain readable.

## Page index

After the empty page header, for each page in ascending pgno order:
`uvarint(pgno) ++ uvarint(offset) ++ uvarint(size)` where `offset` is the page's
byte offset from the file start. A v0.5.2 page uses
`size = 6 + 4 + len(compressed page data)`. A legacy page omits the four-byte
size. The index ends with `uvarint(0)` and a big-endian `u64` index length. The
length includes the elements and terminator, but it excludes its own field.

## Trailer (16 bytes)

`PostApplyChecksum (u64 @0)`, `FileChecksum (u64 @8)`.

## Checksums — CRC64-ISO with the ChecksumFlag

- Hasher: **CRC64 / ISO polynomial `0xD800000000000000`**, matching Go
  `crc64.MakeTable(crc64.ISO)` (reflected; init 0; per-update invert-process-invert).
- `ChecksumFlag = 1 << 63` is OR-ed into **every** stored checksum (so it is never 0).
- `ChecksumPage(pgno, data) = ChecksumFlag | CRC64( BE_u32(pgno) ++ data )`.
- Rolling DB checksum (post-apply): start `ChecksumFlag`, then for each non-lock
  page `chksum = ChecksumFlag | (chksum ^ ChecksumPage(pgno, data))`. Verified
  against the trailer's PostApplyChecksum **only for snapshots**.
- **FileChecksum** = `ChecksumFlag | CRC64(feed)`. The v0.5.2 feed contains the
  header and each page header. It also contains each compressed-size field and
  the corresponding uncompressed page data. It then contains the empty page
  header, the page index with its size field, and the post-apply checksum. The
  compressed page bytes are not part of the feed. A legacy feed omits each
  compressed-size field.

## Filename

`<minTXID:016x>-<maxTXID:016x>.ltx`, e.g. `0000000000000001-0000000000000001.ltx`.

313:     /// Enumerate the fleet membership records used for advisory placement.
314:     /// The adapter owns pagination and bounded I/O concurrency; the core gets
315:     /// every decoded observation and owns all filtering and selection policy.
316:     pub async fn read_capacity_peers(&self) -> anyhow::Result<Vec<CapacityPeer>> {
317:         const READ_CONCURRENCY: usize = 16;
318:         let current_ms = now_ms();
319:         let mut nodes = Vec::new();
320:         for object in self.bucket.list("nodes/").await? {
321:             // A record nothing has rewritten in several lease lifetimes
322:             // belongs to a node that is not coming back. Skipping it here
323:             // is the difference between reading the live fleet and
324:             // reading every node that has ever run: the listing is what
325:             // the placement decision costs, and it is paid on every
326:             // unowned cell.
327:             if !capacity_record_is_recent(
328:                 object.last_modified.timestamp(),
329:                 current_ms,
330:                 self.lease_ttl_ms,
331:             ) {
332:                 continue;
333:             }
334:             let Some(node) = object
335:                 .location
336:                 .as_ref()
337:                 .strip_prefix("nodes/")
338:                 .and_then(|key| key.strip_suffix(".json"))
339:             else {
340:                 continue;
341:             };
342:             if !node.is_empty() {
343:                 nodes.push(node.to_string());
344:             }
345:         }
346:         nodes.sort();
347:         nodes.dedup();
348: 
349:         let mut reads = stream::iter(nodes.into_iter().map(|node| async move {
350:             let key = format!("nodes/{node}.json");
351:             Ok::<_, anyhow::Error>(load_json::<NodeLeaseWire>(&self.bucket, &key).await?.map(
352:                 |(lease, _)| CapacityPeer {
353:                     node: lease.node,
354:                     addr: lease.addr,
355:                     expires_ms: lease.expires_ms,
356:                     peer_protocol: lease.peer_protocol,
357:                     sampled_ms: lease.load.sampled_ms,
358:                     resident_cells: lease.load.resident_cells,
359:                     host_websockets: lease.load.host_websockets,
360:                     rss_bytes: lease.load.rss_bytes,
361:                     in_use_bytes: lease.load.in_use_bytes,
362:                     pressured: lease.load.pressured,
363:                     memory_headroom: lease.load.memory_headroom,
364:                     restoring: lease.load.restoring,
365:                     paced_handoff: lease.paced_handoff,
366:                 },
367:             ))
368:         }))
369:         .buffer_unordered(READ_CONCURRENCY);
370:         let mut peers = Vec::new();
371:         while let Some(peer) = reads.next().await {
372:             if let Some(peer) = peer? {
373:                 peers.push(peer);
374:             }
375:         }
376:         Ok(peers)
377:     }
378: 
379:     /// Publish a cell as unowned, keeping its epoch.
380:     ///
381:     /// Read-then-conditional-write, because the release is only safe against
382:     /// the exact record this node wrote: a takeover in the meantime means the
383:     /// cell is someone else's now, and blanking it would strip a live owner's

87:     /// removed. `None` outside a readable Linux memory cgroup.
88:     pub cgroup_working_set_bytes: Option<u64>,

90:     /// limit constrains, including charges that process RSS does not contain.
91:     /// `None` outside a readable Linux memory cgroup.
92:     pub cgroup_current_bytes: Option<u64>,

95: impl Load {
96:     /// The ordinary pressure measurement. A cgroup working set contains active
97:     /// kernel charges that process RSS omits. Subtract the same measured
98:     /// allocator slack from it, or retained pages would recreate the admission
99:     /// wedge through the cgroup path. The process measurement remains the floor
100:     /// because cgroup and RSS accounting can differ for shared pages.
101:     pub fn memory_bytes(self) -> u64 {
102:         let allocator_slack = self.rss_bytes.saturating_sub(self.in_use_bytes);
103:         let cgroup_in_use = self
104:             .cgroup_working_set_bytes
105:             .unwrap_or_default()
106:             .saturating_sub(allocator_slack);
107:         self.in_use_bytes.max(cgroup_in_use)

109: 
110:     /// The hard pressure measurement. `memory.current` is authoritative when
111:     /// present because the cgroup limit constrains it, not process RSS.
112:     pub fn hard_bytes(self) -> u64 {
113:         self.cgroup_current_bytes.unwrap_or(self.rss_bytes)
114:     }
115: 
116:     pub fn metric_bytes(self, metric: Metric) -> u64 {
117:         match metric {
118:             Metric::InUse => self.memory_bytes(),
119:             Metric::Rss => self.hard_bytes(),

125: /// This is the ordinary case, and shedding relieves it.
126: pub const SHED_MEMORY: &str = "memory";

128: /// The latch engaged because the complete cgroup charge, or the RSS fallback,
129: /// crossed the absolute cap. The string keeps its established telemetry name,
130: /// but a Linux container decides it from `memory.current`.
131: pub const SHED_RSS_HARD: &str = "rss-hard";
132: 
133: impl PressureConfig {
134:     /// Build the watermarks from the machine and the operator's setting.
135:     ///
136:     /// The policy lives here, not at the edge, because it is arithmetic with a
137:     /// correctness argument and requires explicit validation. The shell only
138:     /// supplies the two facts it can read: how much memory the process can use, and what

140:     /// `Some(0)` disables pressure shedding altogether.
141:     ///
142:     /// The absolute cap is 95% of the machine and is never derived from the
143:     /// ceiling. A cap derived from the ceiling either lands above the machine
144:     /// (so it never fires) or below the ceiling (so it fires first on every
145:     /// sample and the classifier is reading the hard measurement again). Both
146:     /// have shipped in this file; neither is a floor.
147:     ///
148:     /// When the machine size is unknown, the cap falls back to 125% of an
149:     /// explicit ceiling. That is worse than a share of the machine and better
150:     /// than no floor at all.
151:     pub fn from_limits(total_memory_bytes: Option<u64>, max_rss_mb: Option<u64>) -> Self {
152:         // A watermark of zero is worse than no watermark: every sample crosses
153:         // it and none can clear it, so the node latches on its first sample and
154:         // refuses every cell for its lifetime. A machine that reports nothing
155:         // usable therefore gets no watermark at all. Linux reports 0 for a
156:         // cgroup limit of `0` and for an unreadable `MemTotal`.
157:         let usable = |bytes: u64| (bytes > 0).then_some(bytes);
158:         let high_bytes = match max_rss_mb {
159:             None => total_memory_bytes.and_then(|total| usable(total / 5 * 4)),
160:             Some(0) => None,
161:             Some(megabytes) => usable(megabytes.saturating_mul(1024 * 1024)),
162:         };
163:         let rss_hard_bytes = high_bytes.and_then(|high| {
164:             // `checked_mul`, because the fallback multiplies an operator's
165:             // number: a saturating multiply followed by a divide would return a
166:             // cap *below* the ceiling, which is the shape this avoids.
167:             let fallback = high.checked_mul(5).map_or(u64::MAX, |scaled| scaled / 4);
168:             let cap = total_memory_bytes
169:                 .and_then(|total| usable(total / 100 * 95))
170:                 .unwrap_or(fallback);
171:             usable(cap)
172:         });
173:         Self {
174:             high_bytes,
175:             rss_hard_bytes,
176:         }
177:     }
178: 
179:     /// Does the ceiling sit at or above the absolute cap?
180:     ///
181:     /// Then the cap is the effective limit and the node decides on its complete
182:     /// cgroup charge or RSS fallback. That is the operator's
183:     /// choice -- they asked for a ceiling above the safety floor -- but it
184:     /// gives up the recovery property of this module, so the shell reports it.
185:     pub fn ceiling_above_cap(self) -> bool {
186:         match (self.high_bytes, self.rss_hard_bytes) {
187:             (Some(high), Some(cap)) => high >= cap,
188:             _ => false,
189:         }
190:     }
191: 
192:     /// Fold a sample into the latches, and say why the node is shedding.
193:     ///
194:     /// Each ceiling latches on its own crossing: it engages at its ceiling and
195:     /// releases at its own low watermark, which is 80% of that ceiling. The
196:     /// hard cap is reported first, because it is the more serious of the two.
197:     ///
198:     /// The latches are carried separately and not derived from the reported
199:     /// reason. Sharing them lets one crossing hold the node against the other's
200:     /// watermark, in either direction: a crossing of the ordinary ceiling then
201:     /// holds the node on a resident-set watermark, which is issue #36 again,
202:     /// and a hard-cap crossing then holds it on a ceiling it never crossed.
203:     pub fn classify(self, s: Load, was: Latches) -> (Latches, Option<&'static str>) {
204:         let over = |ceiling: Option<u64>, sample: u64, latched: bool| {
205:             ceiling.is_some_and(|c| sample >= c || (latched && sample > Self::low_watermark(c)))
206:         };
207:         let latches = Latches {
208:             memory: over(self.high_bytes, s.memory_bytes(), was.memory),
209:             rss_hard: over(self.rss_hard_bytes, s.hard_bytes(), was.rss_hard),
210:         };
211:         let reason = if latches.rss_hard {
212:             Some(SHED_RSS_HARD)
213:         } else if latches.memory {
214:             Some(SHED_MEMORY)
215:         } else {
216:             None
217:         };
218:         (latches, reason)
219:     }
220: 
221:     /// The sample a latched ceiling releases at: 80% of the ceiling.
222:     ///
223:     /// One definition, because two callers read it. `classify` decides whether
224:     /// the latch still holds, and the walk down's stopping condition asks
225:     /// whether shedding can still get the sample down here. Two copies of the
226:     /// arithmetic drift, and a walk down that aims at the wrong number either
227:     /// stops above the line it could have reached or never stops at all.
228:     fn low_watermark(ceiling: u64) -> u64 {
229:         ceiling.saturating_mul(4) / 5
230:     }
231: 
232:     /// Whether the sample leaves the reserve below every configured low
233:     /// watermark. A rollout uses this stricter state instead of `!pressured`:
234:     /// a node can be below the high watermark without enough room to absorb a
235:     /// donor. A disabled ceiling imposes no headroom condition.
236:     pub fn has_headroom(self, sample: Load) -> bool {
237:         let below = |ceiling: Option<u64>, bytes: u64| {
238:             ceiling.is_none_or(|ceiling| bytes <= Self::low_watermark(ceiling))
239:         };
240:         below(self.high_bytes, sample.memory_bytes())
241:             && below(self.rss_hard_bytes, sample.hard_bytes())
242:     }
243: 
244:     /// Where the walk down against `metric` has to get the sample to.
245:     ///
246:     /// `None` means no ceiling is configured for that measurement, so nothing
247:     /// can latch on it and no walk down works against it.
248:     pub fn resume_line(self, metric: Metric) -> Option<u64> {
249:         let ceiling = match metric {
250:             Metric::InUse => self.high_bytes,
251:             Metric::Rss => self.rss_hard_bytes,
252:         };
253:         ceiling.map(Self::low_watermark)
254:     }
255: 
256:     /// Which measurement the walk down must work against, given the latches.
257:     ///
258:     /// The ordinary ceiling wins whenever it is latched, even if the cap is
259:     /// latched too. Eviction relieves the ordinary ceiling and may do nothing
260:     /// at all for the cap, so choosing the cap's measurement while the node is
261:     /// genuinely over its ordinary ceiling stops the walk down exactly when it
262:     /// is needed.
263:     pub fn walk_metric(latches: Latches) -> Metric {
264:         if latches.memory {
265:             Metric::InUse
266:         } else {
267:             Metric::Rss
268:         }
269:     }
270: 
271:     /// How far to shed down to. A memory trigger takes a proportion of what was
272:     /// just measured because the effect of an eviction is not visible until
273:     /// the next sample.
274:     pub fn release_target(resident_cells: usize) -> usize {
275:         resident_cells.saturating_sub((resident_cells / 10).max(1))
276:     }
277: }
278: 
279: pub const MAX_OUTBOUND_PIN_PERCENT: usize = 50;
280: 
281: /// May another cell be pinned resident by an outbound WebSocket?
282: ///
283: /// An outbound socket is not hibernatable, so eviction refuses its cell for as
284: /// long as it is open. That is correct — a live host transport cannot survive
285: /// eviction — but it means every pinned cell is removed from the eviction
286: /// pool. Pin the whole ceiling and a resource walk down has nothing to
287: /// nominate. The budget is node-wide, counted in pinned *cells* rather than
288: /// sockets, because one socket is enough to pin. `ceiling` is the hard resident
289: /// cap.
290: pub fn may_pin_outbound(pinned_cells: usize, ceiling: Option<usize>) -> bool {
291:     ceiling.is_none_or(|cap| {
292:         // At least one, always. The share alone rounds to zero below a ceiling
293:         // of two, which would make an outbound socket impossible on a small
294:         // node rather than merely budgeted.
295:         pinned_cells < (cap.saturating_mul(MAX_OUTBOUND_PIN_PERCENT) / 100).max(1)
296:     })
297: }

# Examples

These small Wrangler projects demonstrate progressively more of the Worker and
Durable Object surface supported by `celld`:

- `hello/` — a stateless Worker `fetch` handler
- `webapi/` — common Web Platform APIs
- `counter/` — a SQLite-backed Durable Object
- `vectordb/` — nearest-color search with a per-object `vec0` index
- `d1/` — a guestbook on a D1 database
- `r2/` — object reads, writes, and deletes on an R2 bucket
- `kv/` — key reads, writes, and deletes in a KV namespace
- `async/` — a timer and asynchronous Durable Object storage
- `body/` — request and response bodies
- `router/` — Worker-to-Durable-Object routing
- `wsecho/` — WebSocket echo with hibernation
- `wsclient/` — outbound WebSocket client from a Durable Object
- `alarm/` — a Durable Object alarm handler
- `cron/` — a cron trigger that logs each tick
- `workflow/` — a Workflow that builds a report in one durable step
- `rpc/` — Durable Object method calls through JS RPC
- `wasm/` — a Durable Object counter in Rust, compiled to Wasm with
  [workers-rs](https://github.com/cloudflare/workers-rs); needs a build step
  first (see its [README](wasm/README.md))

Deploy an example from its directory to the same bucket the nodes use:

```sh
celld deploy . --bucket s3://my-cells-bucket
```

The counter example uses the `name` query parameter as the Durable Object
name. It uses `default` when the parameter is absent. Send requests for
different names to demonstrate independent cells:

```sh
curl 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/increment?name=alpha'
curl 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/increment?name=beta'
curl 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/increment?name=alpha'
```

A fleet can place the named cells on different nodes, and each cell keeps an
independent counter.

They are examples, not the complete compatibility test suite.

---
type: architecture
title: celld system architecture
description: How celld runs Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects as self-hosted cells on your own machines, the three-crate layering, the single-actor decision core, and the primary control and data flows.
tags: [architecture, durable-objects, rust, distributed-systems]
---

# celld system architecture

celld is an open-source daemon that runs Cloudflare Workers and Durable
Objects on machines you own. Each Durable Object is a **cell**: a named
server with its own SQLite database. A node is one `celld` process, and the
nodes that share one bucket are a **fleet**; the bucket holds the
deployments, the cell state, and small ownership records. celld needs no
serving control plane and no consensus service — a conditional bucket write
gives a node ownership of a cell, so exactly one node owns a cell at a time
(README.md#L1-L23).

## Ownership boundaries: a three-crate split

The workspace is deliberately split so that all behavioral decisions live in
one crate and every other crate only executes them:

- **`celld-logic`** (`crates/logic`) is the "clean-sheet celld decision
  core". `on_event` is the only way behavioral state advances; the production
  executor and the deterministic simulator both feed it events and perform
  the returned effects, and no adapter may mutate `State` directly
  (crates/logic/lib.rs#L3-L7). It performs no I/O of its own: the clock, the
  randomness, and the object store are interfaces, and a simulator drives the
  core (docs/testing.md#L88-L95).
- **`celld`** (`crates/celld`) is the effect executor and adapter host. The
  `Cargo.toml` states the contract: "`crates/logic` owns all behavioral state
  and decisions; `crates/celld` is only an effect executor and adapter host"
  (Cargo.toml#L1-L2). It owns the V8 engine, the HTTP listeners, the bucket
  client, the replication executor, and the CLI.
- **`celld-ltx`** (`crates/ltx`) is an embeddable streaming-replication
  library for SQLite: it captures WAL data as LTX segments, reads and writes
  replica storage, restores databases, compacts levels, and reads bundle
  objects. It is a from-scratch Rust reimplementation of Litestream v0.5.11,
  with the block format following LTX v0.5.2 (crates/ltx/src/lib.rs#L3-L13).

The split is what makes the coordination protocol testable: the pure
decision core is replayed by a seeded scheduler, so a failure is not a fluke
(docs/testing.md#L96-L103).

## The execution model

The binary runs one serial actor that is the only caller of
`celld_logic::on_event`. The actor polls its mailbox, timers, and in-flight
effect futures together; adapter futures never borrow core state, and they
send versioned completion events back through the mailbox
(crates/celld/lib.rs#L5-L9). This single-threaded-through-the-core shape is
required so monotonic lease ticks can fence the node even when a storage
operation remains hung, without spawning a task per effect
(crates/celld/main.rs#L7-L13).

The core is an event/effect machine:

- `Event` is the only way in and `Effect` the only way out; both are data
  types defined in `crates/logic/types.rs`
  (crates/logic/types.rs#L401-L402). Events include `Request`, `OwnerRead`,
  `OwnerCasCompleted`, `DurableReached`, `RestoreCompleted`,
  `RuntimeStarted`, `NodeFenced`, and `ReleaseAll`.
- Every asynchronous effect is versioned by an operation id; completion
  events with an obsolete `op` are ignored
  (crates/logic/types.rs#L737-L744). Effects include `ReadOwner`,
  `CasOwner`, `CasNodeLease`, `Restore`, `StartRuntime`, `Publish`,
  `AwaitDurable`, `VerifyOwnership`, `StopRuntime`, `FireAlarm`, and
  `Release`.
- The core stores a channel for each output and hands it back; it never
  reads it. `Channel` enumerates every external route a cell's state can
  leave the process: `Response`, `Fetch`, `WsHibernatable`, `WsSelf`,
  `Service`, `CellRpc`, and `Queue` (crates/logic/types.rs#L334-L354).

## Nodes, fleets, and cells

- **Cell**: one Durable Object — a small server with a name and a private
  SQLite database. Cells share no database; each cell runs on one thread, a
  second request interleaves only while the first awaits, and storage
  operations are synchronous and never interleave
  (docs/README.md#L8-L15).
- **Node**: one `celld` process on one machine. It embeds V8 and executes
  Wrangler bundles (README.md#L16-L18).
- **Fleet**: the nodes that share one bucket. Any node can serve any cell,
  so capacity is added by starting another node against the same bucket
  (docs/README.md#L17-L21). Nodes discover owners and peers from bucket
  leases; there is no account or join service (README.md#L185-L187).
- **The bucket** is the root of authority. It stores the deployments, the
  SQLite replicas, the ownership records, the node leases, and the shared
  peer-authentication secret (docs/security.md#L138-L145). A person who
  holds the bucket credentials controls the fleet.

A cell has the same states as a Cloudflare Durable Object: **resident**
(active or idle in memory), **hibernated** (out of memory but keeping its
hibernatable WebSockets on its node), **inactive** (an object only in the
bucket, owned by nobody), and **remote** (owned by another node). Every cell
starts inactive (docs/README.md#L22-L34).

## Control flow: a request to a cell

A request for a cell enters the actor as an `Event::Request`/`RequestAt`.
The core resolves ownership through its phase machine
(`Phase::ReadingOwner` → `ReadingNodeLease` → `RecoveringOwnerLog` →
`ReadingCapacity` → `WaitingCapacity` → `Acquiring` → `ReconcilingAcquire` →
`Restoring` → `Starting` → `Publishing` → `Resident`; crates/logic/lib.rs#L113-L190),
emitting effects such as `ReadOwner`, `CasOwner`, `Restore`, `StartRuntime`,
and `Publish` that adapters perform. If the cell is owned by another node
the core routes it to a `Remote` phase (crates/logic/lib.rs#L180-L188), and
the adapter proxies the call over the signed peer transport. Management and
inspection traffic reads the same state machine through the
`PresenceSnapshot` projection, which carries each resident cell's exact
fencing epoch (crates/logic/types.rs#L48-L54).

The `Config` type in the core carries the admission ceilings the core
enforces: `max_resident`, `max_activations`, `max_evictions`, `max_releases`,
`max_outbound_websockets`, and the pressure configuration
(crates/logic/types.rs#L62-L136). The shell builds this from the environment
(`crates/celld/machine.rs`) and the core makes every decision from it, so a
deterministic schedule can replay the decisions.

## Data flow: durable writes

Each cell's SQLite database runs in WAL mode. Every committed write is
captured as LTX data and uploaded to the bucket under
`cells/<cell>/ltx/e<epoch>/` with plain unconditional PUTs
(crates/celld/ltx_repl.rs#L10-L15; docs/guarantees.md#L120-L128). The epoch
in the object key is the fence: a node that lost ownership can keep writing,
but its writes land in a superseded prefix, and a restore selects the current
lineage (docs/guarantees.md#L120-L128).

celld does not acknowledge a write until a durability proof covers it
(RPO=0). With `CELLD_DURABILITY=fleet` (the default), the owner sends each
write to one or two follower nodes that fsync it and answers as soon as they
hold it on disk; the bucket upload finishes afterwards. A single node has
nobody to send to, so every write waits for the bucket
(docs/README.md#L51-L59). The output gate withholds each response until the
proof lands (crates/logic/types.rs#L500-L536); see the
[ownership and durability](ownership-and-durability.md) page for the
mechanism.

## Runtime and build entrypoints

- **Binary entry**: `crates/celld/main.rs` (the `celld` binary) and its CLI
  parser `crates/celld/main/cli.rs`. The process uses jemalloc as the global
  allocator, chosen after a measured throughput comparison against glibc
  malloc (crates/celld/main.rs#L44-L50).
- **Library surface**: `crates/celld/lib.rs` re-exports the adapter modules.
  The `celld` crate additionally provides a fair `select!` facade
  (`crates/celld/lib.rs` implements the macro machinery; the documented
  contract is in docs/library-api.md).
- **Release profile**: size-tuned (`opt-level = "s"`, fat LTO, `panic =
  "abort"`, stripped); a `lab` profile trades the fat-LTO relink for thin LTO
  and keeps line tables for `perf` (Cargo.toml#L8-L27).
- **CI**: `.github/workflows/release.yml` builds Linux x86-64, Linux ARM64,
  and Apple Silicon binaries from a `candidate` branch, attests provenance,
  and publishes the container image `ghcr.io/denoland/celld` on a published
  release.

## Two HTTP surfaces

A node opens two HTTP listeners (docs/security.md#L21-L34):

- The **public listener** (`--listen`) serves the deployed Worker. It
  reserves only `/.well-known/celld/health`; the deployed Worker owns every
  other public path.
- The **internal listener** (`--internal-listen`) serves the peer protocol
  and the operator API. Its default address is `127.0.0.1:0`, so celld
  selects an available loopback port at each start; `--advertise` gives
  peers an address that reaches it.

celld does not terminate TLS on either listener; the private network is the
security boundary (docs/security.md#L78-L80). See the
[security](security.md) page for the complete boundary.

## Invariants and failure behavior

- **One writer per cell**: the ownership records use conditional writes, so
  two nodes cannot acquire one cell, and each activation advances the epoch,
  so an epoch never has two writers (docs/guarantees.md#L108-L118).
- **RPO=0**: a write is acknowledged only after a durability proof covers
  it; a failed or ambiguous proof refuses the response
  (crates/logic/types.rs#L500-L536).
- **Lease-based self-fencing**: each node holds a lease in the bucket that it
  renews after one third of its lifetime; when the published expiry passes,
  the node fences itself, fails its outstanding requests, and exits with
  code 3 (docs/guarantees.md#L201-L224).
- **Operation deadlines**: a non-restore operation is bounded by
  `CELLD_OPERATION_DEADLINE_MS` (default 15000), so a swallowed effect cannot
  park a request forever (crates/logic/types.rs#L112-L120).

## Extension seams

- The **decision core** is the seam for protocol change: add an `Event`,
  an `Effect`, and a phase transition in `crates/logic`, then implement the
  effect in an adapter. The deterministic simulator and the TLA+
  specifications are the verification companions (docs/testing.md).
- The **`LtxHost`/`FileSystem` abstraction** in `celld-ltx` lets the
  replication library run against real files or a deterministic fake
  (crates/ltx/src/lib.rs#L51-L54).
- The **`DurabilityOwner`** seam in `crates/celld/node_log.rs` is the
  documented lifetime contract for embedding celld as a library
  (docs/library-api.md#L12-L60).
- **Reserved Durable Object classes** (`__D1Database`, `__Workflow`,
  `__KvNamespace`, `__Queue`) let D1, Workflows, KV, and Queues run as cells
  supplied by the runtime rather than by the Worker
  (crates/celld/deploy.rs#L58-L81).

## Tests that pin the architecture

The crate split is exercised by the conformance and simulation suites: the
`celld` crate includes simulation tests behind `celld_internal_tests` that
drive the same decision core with a simulated store and a simulated clock
(crates/celld/lib.rs#L394-L418), and `crates/logic` is a pure decision core
with no I/O of its own specifically so a simulator can drive it
(docs/testing.md#L88-L95).

claims.statement: The workspace splits decision logic from execution: crates/logic owns all behavioral state and decisions, and crates/celld is only an effect executor and adapter host.

celld-logic is a pure decision core: on_event is the only way behavioral state advances, the production executor and deterministic simulator both feed it events and perform the returned effects, and no adapter may mutate State directly.

The celld executable runs one serial actor that is the only caller of celld_logic::on_event; adapter futures never borrow core state and send versioned completion events back through the actor's mailbox.

The single actor polls its mailbox, timers, and in-flight effect futures together, a shape required so monotonic lease ticks can fence the node even when a storage operation remains hung, without spawning a task per effect.
celld-ltx is an embeddable streaming-replication library for SQLite, a from-scratch Rust reimplementation of Litestream v0.5.11 with the block format following LTX v0.5.2.
The core is an event/effect machine: Event is the only way in and Effect the only way out, both defined as data in crates/logic/types.rs.
Every asynchronous effect is versioned by an operation id; completion events with an obsolete op are ignored.
A node is one celld process and the nodes that share one bucket are a fleet; any node can serve any cell, and cells share no database.
The fleet bucket is the root of fleet authority: it stores the deployments, the SQLite replicas, the ownership records, the node leases, and the shared peer-authentication secret.

A cell's committed SQLite writes are captured as LTX data and uploaded to the bucket under cells/<cell>/ltx/e<epoch>/, and the epoch in the object key is the fence that keeps a stale owner's later writes in a superseded prefix.

The decision core routes a request through a phase machine (reading owner, reading node lease, acquiring, restoring, starting, publishing, resident) and places a cell owned by another node in a Remote phase.
The core Config type carries the admission ceilings the core enforces, including max_resident, max_activations, max_evictions, max_releases, max_outbound_websockets, and the pressure configuration.
The celld process uses jemalloc as its global allocator, chosen after a measured throughput comparison against glibc malloc on a 16-core host.
A node opens two HTTP listeners: the public listener serves the deployed Worker and reserves only /.well-known/celld/health, while the internal listener serves the peer protocol and the operator API.
Each node holds a bucket lease it renews after one third of its lifetime; when its published expiry passes the node fences itself, fails its outstanding requests, and exits with code 3.
A non-restore operation is bounded by CELLD_OPERATION_DEADLINE_MS (default 15000), so a swallowed effect cannot park a request forever.
The runtime supplies four reserved Durable Object classes, __D1Database, __Workflow, __KvNamespace, and __Queue, so D1, Workflows, KV, and Queues run as cells rather than as Worker code.
The crate split is exercised by simulation and conformance suites behind the celld_internal_tests cfg that drive the same decision core with a simulated store and a simulated clock.

3: //! Whether a failed peer dispatch may be re-sent.
4: //!
5: //! A cell runs on exactly one node, so every other node forwards to the

7: //! options: fail the caller, or re-send and risk running the request twice.
8: //! The deciding fact is how far the attempt got. A connection that was never
9: //! established carried no request bytes, so the owner's cell is untouched and
10: //! a fresh attempt cannot double-apply. Every other failure — a timeout after
11: //! the request was written, a truncated body, a decode error — leaves the
12: //! outcome ambiguous: the owner may have run it and lost the reply. Re-sending
13: //! those would break at-most-once execution.
14: //!
15: //! The case this exists for is a burst of cold activations, where TCP
16: //! handshakes stall past the client's connect timeout. Those forwards never
17: //! reached the owner, so surfacing them to the caller is a self-inflicted
18: //! error.

21: #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
22: pub enum Attempt {
23:     /// The peer answered that it no longer owns the cell. Nothing ran.
24:     NotOwner,
25:     /// The connection was never established. No bytes reached the owner.
26:     NeverConnected,
27:     /// The request was on the wire when the attempt failed. The owner may or

30: }
